Block 63 computed a restricted logit lens. It took the original model's hidden states at layers 12–26 on 150 DEV reference solutions and scored each reference token against the model's top-20 candidates, by token category: copied number, computed result, new number, digit continuation, line-start word, other word. Block 64 was the sink-write check. The kernel should still hold the logit-lens accumulator `acc`.

I will reprint its summary and record it in the notes. A clear rise and then fall of reference-token log-probability across the late layers, especially on result digits, would point to a late brake to localize. A monotone climb to the final layer would close the "late brake / overthinking" line.

The eval instruction is not a trigger. On the same 256 reference solutions, the eval prompt (V1) gives the best log-probability: problem-only is 0.14 nats/token worse and "Solve step by step." 0.09 worse, almost entirely on wording, while digits differ by at most 0.025 nats. The format instruction helps the model predict GSM8K-style text rather than holding it back, so the eval-trigger line is closed.

That brings me back to D1, the one edit with a big behavioural effect. It turned the "Let $x$…" LaTeX/algebra mode into markdown and cut loops from 58 to 21 and marker failures sharply, which looks like a restored "base-model" style, but accuracy did not move. One explanation is that the math direction carries both a mode signal and useful math content, so D1 removed a brake and damaged computation at the same time.

I will test this cheaply on the existing pass-5 texts. I parse every explicit binary calculation ("a op b = c") in the original and the D1 answers, and compare how often they are written and how often they are correct. If D1 answers make clearly more arithmetic slips, D1 damaged computation, and a cleaner "mode" direction that spares math content is worth building. If arithmetic accuracy is unchanged, D1 simply changed style, and the remaining deficit lies in problem understanding.

The parse suggests arithmetic is less clean than my notes said. In the original model 18.8% of explicit "a op b = c" calculations come out wrong (21.9% of answers contain at least one), against 12.1% under D1, which also writes fewer equations. But my regex also counts the tail of chained expressions ("2 + 3 + 4 = 9" read as "3 + 4 = 9"), which inflates the error rate, especially in the equation-heavy LaTeX style.

I will exclude matches preceded by an operator and print a few of the remaining "wrong" calculations with short context. A genuine arithmetic error rate around 10–20% would be a concrete, measurable failure to localize (number computation, e.g. at the "=" token). If it falls to a few percent once the chains are excluded, arithmetic is fine, as previously noted, and the deficit is in problem understanding.
